Taking office in December 1983, this Argentine lawyer and social democrat was the first democratically elected president after the country's military 'National Reorganization Process' — who was he?
Raúl Alfonsín: President of Argentina from 1983 to 1989.
Deposed in a 2017 coup after ruling Zimbabwe for 37 years as both prime minister and president, who was this revolutionary-turned-leader?
Robert Mugabe: Leader of Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017.
In 2023 this German politician walked out of The Left to found a Eurosceptic populist party bearing her own name — which firebrand was she?

Depicted in reliefs at Ramesses III's mortuary temple, this mysterious maritime confederation was long blamed for Late Bronze Age raids on Egypt around 1200 BC, though scholars now see them more as a symptom of the era's collapse than its cause. Who were they?
Sea Peoples: Purported ancient tribal confederation of the Late Bronze Age.
Born Farid Khan, this 16th-century ruler founded an empire after defeating the Mughals and made Delhi his capital, earning the title 'the Just King' — who is he?
Sher Shah Suri: Sultan of Hindustan from 1540 to 1545.
Succeeding his father David as king of ancient Israel, this biblical ruler's wealth and foreign wives allegedly introduced idolatry, sowing the seeds for the kingdom's later split. Who is he?
Solomon: Biblical monarch of ancient Israel. The successor of his father David, he is described as the penultimate ruler of all Twelve Tribes of Israel under a united Israel and Judah.
Commonly called "SBY," this retired general was only the second military man after Suharto to become Indonesia's president, serving two terms from 2004 — who is he?

Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono: President of Indonesia from 2004 to 2014. Yudhoyono won the 2004 presidential election—the first direct presidential election in Indonesia, defeating incumbent President Megawati Sukarnoputri.
In Greek mythology, this minor deity personified death itself, and was known to the Romans as Mors or Letum — who is he?
Thanatos: Ancient Greek personification of death.

Nicknamed 'The Tiger of Malaya' after conquering the peninsula and a nearby island stronghold in just 70 days, this WWII Japanese general later held out on Luzon until his country's surrender in 1945 — who is he?
Tomoyuki Yamashita: Japanese officer and war criminal (1885–1946)
In Norse belief, these female figures guide fallen warriors to Odin's hall, sometimes shown accompanied by ravens, swans, or wolves — what are they called?
This American divorcée's romance with Britain's king forced his abdication in 1936 rather than let her become queen — who was she?
Wallis Simpson: Wife of Prince Edward, Duke of Windsor (1896–1986)

One of three brothers with distinguished military careers, this British general rose to Commander-in-Chief, America, during the War of Independence after famously scaling the cliffs at Quebec in 1759. Who was he?
William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe: British Army officer and politician (1729–1814)

Rooted in pre-Islamic Kurdish tradition and shaped by Sufi influence, this monotheistic faith reveres a 'Peacock Angel' as chief among seven angels tasked with guarding the world — which religion is it?
The eldest child of Alfred the Great, this Anglo-Saxon noblewoman ruled the Mercians in her own right from 911 until her death in 918 — who was she?
Æthelflæd: Ruler of Mercia in England from 911 to 918.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Franz Reichelt (born 1878) is the earliest of the four. The parachute failed to deploy and he plummeted 57 metres (187 ft) to his death.
Which of these four began earliest?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 (founded 1937) is the earliest of the four.
Perl (founded 1987) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Horace Bénédict de Saussure is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
Dolph Lundgren is a chemist. Hans "Dolph" Lundgren (Swedish: [ˈdɔlːf ˈlɵ̌nːdɡreːn]; born 3 November 1957) is a Swedish-American actor, filmmaker, and martial artist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiquadium?
Unbiquadium, also known as element 124 or eka-uranium, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has placeholder symbol Ubq and atomic number 124.
In what year was Gabor Maté born?
Gabor Maté ( GAH-bor MAH-tay; born January 1944) is a Canadian physician and author.
In what year was Linus Torvalds born?
Linus Torvalds: Linus Benedict Torvalds (born 28 December 1969) is a Finnish and American software engineer who is the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991.
In what year was John Money born?
John Money: Money researched paraphilia, including pedophilia, and pioneered the use of drug treatment to extinguish the libido of sex offenders.
In what year did Luke the Evangelist die?
Luke the Evangelist was one of the Four Evangelists—the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels.
In what year did Charles Babbage die?
Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 – 18 October 1871) was an English polymath.
In what year was Glutathione discovered?
Glutathione (GSH,) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.
In what year was Morphine discovered?
Morphine, formerly known as morphium, is an opiate found naturally in opium, a dark brown resin produced by drying the latex of opium poppies (Papaver somniferum).
Acetylcysteine: Pfizer. It has been used to treat lactobezoar in infants.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-35 from?
Sukhoi Su-35: Soviet Union. The type was originally developed by the Soviet Union from the Su-27 and was known as the Su-27M.
Who is credited with discovering Palladium?
Palladium: William Hyde Wollaston. Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Who is credited with discovering Pectin?
Pectin: Henri Braconnot. The principal chemical component of pectin is galacturonic acid (a sugar acid derived from galactose).
Who is credited with discovering Oxygen?
Oxygen: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas owes its straight-line shape to a carbon-carbon triple bond — and though pure it's odorless, commercial grades reek thanks to impurities. What is it?
Acetylene (systematic name: ethyne) is a chemical compound with the formula C2H2 and structure HCCH.

Native to South America but cultivated in Europe since the 17th century for its fragrant oil, this flowering member of the verbena family is better known by a common name referencing a citrus fruit — what's its scientific name?
Aloysia citrodora is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family Verbenaceae, native to South America.

Named in 1835 from the Greek for 'flower' and 'dark blue,' these pH-shifting pigments paint blueberries, black rice, and some autumn leaves anything from red to purple to nearly black — what are they?

Anthocyanin (from Ancient Greek (nthos) 'flower' and / (kuneos/kuanos) 'dark blue'), also called anthocyans, are water-soluble vacuolar pigments that, depending on their pH, may appear red, pink, purple, blue, or black.
With atomic number 85 and symbol At, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, forming only as a decay product of heavier elements — name it?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
Recorded in an ancient Chinese herbal medicine text from around 200 BC and named for a barberry-related plant genus, this yellow-pigmented alkaloid glows under ultraviolet light. What compound is it?
Berberine is an organic compound classified as benzylisoquinoline alkaloid.
Unlike most elements, this one is made almost entirely by cosmic ray collisions rather than inside stars, making it rare despite its light atomic weight. What element is it (symbol B)?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
The very same compound that hardens eggshells, builds pearls, and forms the chalk on a classroom board can also be swallowed as an antacid to calm an upset stomach — what is it?
Calcium carbonate is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CaCO3.
This set of metabolic reactions oxidizes biological fuels using an electron acceptor like oxygen to produce ATP, the molecule that stores usable chemical energy in cells — what is it?

Cellular respiration is the process of oxidizing biological fuels using an inorganic electron acceptor, such as oxygen, to drive production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which stores chemical energy in a biologically accessible form.

An organic compound found naturally in citrus fruits with the formula C6H8O7, over two million tons are manufactured annually for use as an acidifier, flavoring, and preservative. What is this compound?
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7. In biochemistry, it is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, which occurs in the metabolism of all aerobic organisms.
Lending its metal to sterling silver, cupronickel coins, and strain-gauge alloys, this element carries atomic number 29 and a name drawn from the Latin 'cuprum' — what is it?
Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu (from Latin cuprum) and atomic number 29.

He's the only person to have won BAFTAs in black-and-white, colour, high-definition, 3D and 4K — a broadcasting career that began way back in 1954 hosting Zoo Quest. Who is this English natural historian?
David Attenborough (born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
What flying insect, of which about 3,000 species exist, is known for its large compound eyes, two pairs of transparent wings, and often iridescent, metallic body coloration?
Dragonfly is a flying insect belonging to the infraorder Anisoptera below the order Odonata.
Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows elsewhere in the body—often on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or pelvis—affecting roughly 10% of women of reproductive age worldwide. What is this condition?
Endometriosis is a disease in which tissue similar to the endometrium - the lining of the uterus (womb) - grows elsewhere in the body.
Every member of this mammal family is an obligate carnivore with retractile claws and a powerful bite, from forest dwellers to desert hunters — which family is it?
Felidae is the family of mammals in the order Carnivora colloquially referred to as cats.
Co-author of 'The Communist Manifesto' and lifelong collaborator with Karl Marx, this German theorist finished the second and third volumes of 'Das Kapital' after his partner's death — who is he?
Friedrich Engels (28 November 1820 - 5 August 1895) was a German philosopher, social and political theorist, journalist, businessman, and revolutionary socialist.

Colorless, odorless, and oddly sweet, this viscous sugar alcohol carries three hydroxyl groups, forms the backbone of every triglyceride in animal fat, and moonlights as a food sweetener — what is it?
Glycerol is a sugar alcohol with chemical formula C3H5(OH)3.

In 1896 this English physician dosed himself with mescaline and wrote one of the first public reports of the trip; he also co-wrote English's first medical textbook on homosexuality and coined the term 'narcissism' — who was he?
Havelock Ellis (2 February 1859 - 8 July 1939) was an English physician, eugenicist, writer, progressive intellectual and social reformer who studied human sexuality.
Found from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego across roughly 375 species, the males of this American bird family boast the most diverse plumage colors of any birds — what are they?
Hummingbird are birds native to the Americas and comprise the biological family Trochilidae.

This pathogen has caused seasonal flu in humans and also infects birds and some mammals; strains circulate constantly in bats, pigs, horses, and dogs. It was the cause of the Spanish Flu pandemic from 1918 to 1920. What is it?
Influenza A virus is a pathogen with strains that cause seasonal flu in humans; it can also infect birds and some mammals.
This British chemical engineer founded and leads a global chemicals conglomerate in 1998, and was briefly the richest person in the UK before shifting his tax residence to Monaco. Who is he?
Jim Ratcliffe (born 18 October 1952) is a British billionaire, chemical engineer, and businessman.

First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two fundamental equalities govern how current and voltage behave in an electrical network, building on Georg Ohm's earlier work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws are two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference (commonly known as voltage) in the lumped element model of electrical circuits.
This American computer scientist rose to prominence after Elon Musk praised his MIT study on Tesla's semi-autonomous driving system, and now hosts a long-form interview podcast. Who is he?
Lex Fridman (born 15 August 1983) is an American computer scientist and podcaster.
Enclosed in a fibrous capsule and linked throughout the body by lymphatic vessels, these kidney-shaped organs filter foreign particles and house the immune system's B and T cells — what are they?
Lymph node is a kidney-shaped organ of the lymphatic system and the adaptive immune system.
This genus of flowering plants belongs to the chamomile tribe of the sunflower family, and several of its species go by the folk name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Matricaria is a genus of flowering plants in the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family.

Usually white but sometimes tinged yellow or pink, this liquid food produced by mammary glands is the primary source of nutrition for young mammals, with its very first production called colostrum — name the substance?
Milk is usually a white liquid food (but can be shades of yellow, cream, pink, or brown) produced by the mammary glands of lactating mammals.

This condition, an inflammation of the heart muscle itself, can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, and irregular heartbeat, and may progress to heart failure if it leads to chronic remodeling of the heart — name the condition?

Myocarditis is inflammation of the cardiac muscle. Myocarditis can progress to inflammatory cardiomyopathy when there is associated ventricular remodeling and cardiac dysfunction due to chronic inflammation.
This American nuclear-capable subsonic stealth bomber, solely operated by the US Air Force, is designed as a flying wing to penetrate sophisticated air defenses. What is this aircraft?
Northrop B-2 Spirit is an American nuclear-capable subsonic stealth strategic bomber, often referred to as a "stealth bomber", solely operated by the United States Air Force.
Atomic number 8 and a potent oxidizing agent, this element pairs up into a colorless, odorless diatomic gas and tops the list of elements in Earth's crust — what is it?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.

Which American chemist was the first to synthesize physostigmine and pioneered making progesterone and testosterone from plant sterols — even starting a company to extract steroid intermediates from wild Mexican yams?
Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899 - April 19, 1975) was an American research chemist and a pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants.

Despite its fearsome reputation as a ferocious predator, this South American freshwater fish actually eats a varied diet that includes plant material, making it more omnivore than monster — what fish is it?
Piranha (or) is any of a number of freshwater fish species in the subfamily Serrasalminae, of the family Serrasalmidae, in the order Characiformes.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.

Named for the ragged appearance of its leaves, this genus of flowering plants native mainly to North America has become an invasive nuisance in parts of Europe due to climate change — what plant is it?
Ragweed are flowering plants in the genus Ambrosia in the aster family, Asteraceae.
Known by the common name 'dog rose,' this climbing wild rose species is native across Europe and stretches into northwest Africa and western Asia — which species?
Rosa canina is a variable climbing, wild rose species native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia.

These pinnipeds, distinguished from true seals by their external ear flaps and ability to walk on all fours, belong to the eared-seal family alongside fur seals, with six living species worldwide. What animal is this?
Sea lion are pinnipeds characterized by external ear flaps, long foreflippers, the ability to walk on all fours, short and thick hair, and a big chest and belly.
Despite the name, this digestive organ is about 6.5 metres long; it's just narrower in diameter than its large counterpart. What organ is it?
Small intestine is an organ in the gastrointestinal tract where most of the absorption of nutrients from food takes place.
This Taiwanese-American software engineer co-founded and served as CTO of a massively popular video-sharing platform before later building MixBit through his company AVOS Systems — who is he?
Steve Chen (Wade-; born August 25, 1978) is a Taiwanese-American software engineer and Internet entrepreneur who is a co-founder and ex-CTO of YouTube.
Modern practitioners prioritize common ancestry as they sort living things into ranked taxa, from domain and kingdom all the way down to species — which biological discipline does this?

Taxonomy (biology) (from Ancient Greek (taxis) 'arrangement' and - (-nomia) 'method') is the scientific study of naming, defining (circumscribing) and classifying groups of biological organisms based on shared characteristics.
Joining Bethesda Game Studios in 1994, this video game director has since led development of both The Elder Scrolls and Fallout series, as well as 2023's Starfield. Who is he?
Todd Howard (born 1970) is an American video game designer, director, and producer who serves as director and executive producer at Bethesda Game Studios.
Native to cool climates across the Northern Hemisphere, this low shrub bears small, round, edible fruit of a deep blue color, and goes by several folk names depending on region — what's the species?
Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, and whortleberry.
The first-ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, this German scientist discovered a form of electromagnetic radiation named after him in some languages — who was he?

Wilhelm Röntgen (27 March 1845 - 10 February 1923) was a German experimental physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays (known as Rntgen rays in many languages).
This Andalusi polymath built a model of the planets' motion, devised colourless glass, made reading lenses, and is even said to have attempted flight — who was this 9th-century inventor?
Abbas ibn Firnas: 9th-century astronomer and physician.
People with this anxiety disorder dread places they feel they can't safely escape — crowds, queues, public transit — and in severe cases become unable to leave home at all. What is it?
Agoraphobia: Anxiety disorder. Agoraphobia is believed to be due to a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
A succulent from the Arabian Peninsula, this popular potted plant stores a soothing gel of acemannan in its leaves — alongside a toxic compound called aloin. What is it?
Aloe vera: Species of plant. It is widely distributed, and is considered an invasive species in many world regions.
Struck off the medical register for 'serious professional misconduct,' this former surgeon authored the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper falsely tying the MMR vaccine to autism — who is he?
The average adult sheds 50 to 70 billion cells a day through this tidy, programmed cell death — named from a Greek word for 'falling off' — quite unlike messy, traumatic necrosis. What is it?
Apoptosis: Form of programmed cell death. Because apoptosis cannot stop once it has begun, it is a highly regulated process.
From the Greek for 'lack of order,' this neurological sign involves loss of voluntary muscle coordination, often linked to cerebellum dysfunction — what is it called?
Ataxia: Neurological impairment of voluntary muscle movement.
Originating in Central Africa, this hunting dog breed doesn't bark but makes an unusual yodel-like sound instead, earning it a nickname — what breed is it?
Basenji: Central African breed of dog. The Fédération Cynologique Internationale places it in the Spitz and "primitive types" categories, while the American Kennel Club classifies it as a hound.
Also known as vitamin B7, this B vitamin is found in every living cell and is popularly sold as a supplement; isolated, it's a white needle-like crystal — what is it?
Biotin: Chemical compound and essential nutrient.

Completely dependent on humans for reproduction after millennia of selective breeding, this domesticated moth's caterpillars produce the raw fiber behind a 5,000-year-old Chinese industry — which species?
Bombyx mori: Moth mainly used in the production of silk.

Prescribed under the tongue, as a cheek film, an injection, a skin patch, or an implant, this opioid treats pain and opioid use disorder — often combined with naloxone in Suboxone to deter injection misuse. What is it?
Buprenorphine: Opioid used to treat pain and opioid use disorder.
Called 'rockmelon' in Australia and 'spanspek' in South Africa, this orange-fleshed true melon goes by yet another name in North America — what fruit is it?
Cantaloupe: Variety of melon. Originally, cantaloup referred to the true cantaloupe or European cantaloupe with non- to slightly netted and often ribbed rind.
Sold under the brand name Rocephin, this injectable third-generation antibiotic treats everything from meningitis to gonorrhea — which drug?
Ceftriaxone: Antibiotic medication. Ceftriaxone, sold under the brand name Rocephin, is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
The only member of the onion genus native to both the New World and Old World, this perennial herb has edible leaves and flowers and doubles as a natural insect repellent — what is it?
Chives: Species of flowering plant in the family Amaryllidaceae.
With a coat of dusky-grey blotches that inspired its common name, this wild cat is one of the few able to climb down tree trunks head-first, using a long tail for balance — what species is it?

Clouded leopard: Species of wild cat. Its head-and-body length ranges from 68.6 to 108 cm (27.0 to 42.5 in) with a 61 to 91 cm (24 to 36 in) long tail, which it uses for balancing when moving in trees.
Often defined as the transmission of information, this concept is famously modeled as a source encoding a message, sending it through a channel, and a receiver decoding it — what is it?
Communication: Transmission of information. Models of communication are simplified overviews of its main components and their interactions.
Unknown in the wild, this cultivated autumn-flowering plant has had its dried stigmas prized as the world's priciest spice for over 3,500 years — what is its scientific name?
Crocus sativus: Species of flowering plant. Crocus sativus, commonly known as saffron crocus or autumn crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae.
Introduced in 1984, this turboprop regional airliner series was developed from an earlier company model and later gained 'Quiet' variants with active noise-cancellation — which aircraft family?

De Havilland Canada Dash 8: Canadian turboprop airliner. The De Havilland Canada DHC-8, commonly known as the Dash 8, is a series of turboprop-powered regional airliners, introduced by de Havilland Canada (DHC) in 1984.

The largest collection of fossils from this extinct Ice Age canine came from the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles, though it roamed from South American savanna to North American forested mountains — what animal was it?
Dire wolf: Extinct species of canine mammal.
Its name comes from the Greek word for 'house,' and it studies organisms from the level of a single individual all the way up to the entire biosphere — which branch of biology is it?
Ecology: Study of organisms and their environment.

This is the process of creating economic value by spotting and commercializing opportunities — typically demanding considerable initiative and bearing real risk in exchange for most of the reward. What's the term?
Entrepreneurship: Taking financial risks in the hope of profit.
Also known by the scientific name Gyps fulvus, this large Old World bird of prey belongs to the family Accipitridae — which species is it?
Eurasian griffon vulture: Species of bird. It is also known as the Eurasian griffon or griffon vulture, although the latter term is sometimes used for the genus Gyps as a whole.
This Swiss thinker, alongside Charles Sanders Peirce, is considered one of the two founders of semiotics — the field he himself called 'semiology' — who is he?
Ferdinand de Saussure: Swiss linguist and philosopher (1857–1913)
With a bushy tail, triangular ears, and a reputation for cunning that echoes through folklore worldwide, which small omnivorous canid lives on every continent except Antarctica?
Also known as the Indian bison, this Vulnerable-listed bovine is the largest living member of the wild cattle family, with most of its roughly 21,000 individuals found in India — what animal is it?
Gaur: Largest species of the bovid family.
The simplest and only non-chiral of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids, this compound makes up about 35% of collagen's amino acid content — what is it?
Glycine: Amino acid. In the body, glycine plays several crucial roles.
Also nicknamed the millionfish, this livebearing freshwater fish is one of the world's most popular aquarium species — which fish?

This airway symptom — blood or blood-streaked mucus coughed up from the lungs or throat — turns dangerous mainly because of choking rather than blood loss once it passes 300 milliliters. What is it called?

The only birds whose first two neck vertebrae are fused together, these Old World birds have a long down-curved bill sometimes topped with a bony casque, and share an ecological niche with toucans in the Americas — which birds?
Hornbill: Family of birds. The family is omnivorous, feeding on fruit and small animals.
About the size of an almond in humans, this brain structure links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland — what is it?
Hypothalamus: Area of the brain below the thalamus.
Symbol Fe, atomic number 26, it's the most common element on Earth by mass and forms much of the planet's core — yet smelting it needs furnaces 500°C hotter than copper does. Which metal?
Iron: Chemical element with atomic number 26 (Fe)
With Emmanuelle Charpentier, this Berkeley biochemist proposed in 2012 that CRISPR-Cas9 could edit genomes — work that won them the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry; who is she?
Jennifer Doudna: American biochemist and Nobel laureate (born 1964)
Nicknamed the 'miracle leaf' and 'life plant,' this Madagascar-native succulent sprouts tiny new plantlets right along the edges of its leaves — which species?

Kalanchoe pinnata: Succulent plant native to Madagascar. Kalanchoe pinnata, commonly known as cathedral bells, air plant, life plant, miracle leaf, and love bush, is a succulent plant native to Madagascar.
Once a water retriever in Italy's Po Delta marshlands, this Italian dog breed later became prized for sniffing out truffles — which breed?
Lagotto Romagnolo: Italian breed of dog.
This fibrous connective tissue links bone to bone in every one of the 30,000 known amniote species, and in birds it even anchors flight feathers to bone — what is it?

This Canadian physicist worked on the Manhattan Project determining critical mass values for uranium and plutonium, and in 1946 was fatally exposed to radiation in a lab accident at Los Alamos — who is he?
Louis Slotin: Canadian physicist and chemist (1910–1946)
Nicknamed sea cows, these slow-moving herbivorous mammals graze on more than 60 kinds of aquatic plants in the Caribbean, the Amazon basin, and West Africa — what are they?
Manatee: Genus of mammals. The main causes of death for manatees are human-related issues, such as habitat destruction and human objects.

Spanning everything from sacred religious writings to the exuberantly profane, and often grouped by place, language, and genre, what broad body of European writing falls between late antiquity and the Renaissance?
Medieval literature: Literary works of the Middle Ages.
Grouped by their small size and use of echolocation, this suborder of flying mammals turns out to be genetically distinct from its bigger, fruit-eating relatives — which creatures?

Thought to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' and a reduced risk of inbreeding-linked health problems, this catch-all term covers roughly 150 million dogs worldwide that don't belong to any officially recognized breed — what's it called?
This arthropod subphylum includes millipedes and centipedes, and one of its earliest fossils preserves the first known evidence of animals breathing air on land. What's the group called?
Myriapoda: Subphylum of arthropods. The group contains about 13,000 species, all of them terrestrial.
This Serbian-American engineer designed the modern alternating current electricity supply system—the backbone of today's power grid. Who?
Nikola Tesla: Serbian-American engineer and inventor (1856–1943)

This family of 138 primate species — including baboons, macaques, and mandrills — split off from a separate lineage of primates some 45 to 55 million years ago, yet is the closer kin to apes of the two — which family?
Old World monkey: Family of mammals. Old World monkey genera include baboons (genus Papio), red colobus (genus Piliocolobus), and macaques (genus Macaca).
A pale-blue gas with a chlorine-like pungent odour, this unstable three-atom cousin of oxygen forms by UV light and electrical discharges and shields us high in the stratosphere — what is it?
Nicknamed "javelina" or "skunk pig," this social New World mammal travels in herds called squadrons and counts true pigs as its closest living relatives — what pig-like ungulate is it?
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive fear that persists more than six months and can trigger fainting in blood-or-injury cases — what is it?
Phobia: Anxiety disorder classified by a persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
First synthesized in 1940 by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons at UC Berkeley, this radioactive metal can expand up to 70% in volume when its surface oxidizes — which element?
Plutonium: Chemical element with atomic number 94 (Pu)
Though often mistaken for a true antelope, this hoofed North American mammal is actually the last living member of its own family, and its closest relatives are the giraffe and okapi — which animal?

Pronghorn: Species of North American hoofed mammal. The pronghorn (UK:, US:) (Antilocapra americana) is a species of artiodactyl (even-toed, hoofed) mammal indigenous to interior western and central North America.
Named for its four heads, this large muscle group covers the front of the thigh and is the sole muscle that extends the knee — what is it?
Quadriceps: Group of human leg muscle.

Also known as Willis–Ekbom disease, this neurological disorder creates an overwhelming urge to move one's limbs, especially when at rest, often described as a crawling or tingling sensation — what's the condition called?
Restless legs syndrome: Medical condition. There is often an unpleasant feeling in the legs that improves temporarily by moving them.
Also known as sixth disease, this childhood viral infection typically strikes before age three with a sudden fever followed by a pink rash lasting under three days — what's the condition called?
Roseola: Human disease caused by human herpesviruses.
This Indian-American executive became CEO of a major tech company in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, after leading its cloud and enterprise division — who is he?
In this biological process, haploid gametes such as sperm and egg cells combine to form a zygote that develops into a diploid organism — what is it called?
Sexual reproduction: Biological process. Sexual reproduction is the most common life cycle in multicellular eukaryotes, such as animals, fungi and plants.

Once extracted from the ashes of certain salt-absorbing plants and now produced from ordinary salt and limestone via the Solvay process, this alkaline compound is also known as washing soda or soda ash — what is it?
Sodium carbonate: Chemical compound. Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.
Known for a synchronized aerial swarming display called murmuration, this glossy-plumed bird family includes talkative mynas as members — which birds?
Starling: Family of birds. The Sturnidae are named for the genus Sturnus, which in turn comes from the Latin word for starling, sturnus.
This South African biologist made a tiny roundworm, C. elegans, the model organism for studying how bodies develop, sharing a 2002 Nobel for the work — who is he?
